concept: India under East India Company’s Rule
question: Colonial economic policies created a skewed distribution of income and wealth in Indian society. Which of the following is a key indicator of income inequality in colonial India?
solution:
The correct answer is __**Unequal land ownership patterns**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Unequal land ownership patterns** were one of the most prominent indicators of income inequality in colonial India.
 
• The **British land revenue systems**, such as the **Permanent Settlement** (introduced in 1793) and **Ryotwari system**, created a class of landlords who held vast tracts of land, while the majority of the population consisted of poor tenant farmers or laborers.
 
• Landlords often exploited tenants by charging exorbitant rents, further deepening economic disparities.
 
• The lack of access to land for the majority of the population meant that wealth was concentrated in the hands of a few individuals or families.
 
• This skewed distribution of land ownership perpetuated poverty and reduced economic mobility for a large segment of Indian society during the colonial period.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Colonial economic policies:**

 
 
• The British economic policies in India were primarily extractive and exploitative, aimed at benefiting the colonial rulers rather than the Indian population.
 
• These policies included high taxation, forced commercialization of agriculture, and minimal investment in industrial development.
 
• The introduction of the **Permanent Settlement** in Bengal was a pivotal moment in creating a landlord class that held disproportionate wealth and power.
 
 
 
• **Other Indicators of Income Inequality:**
 
 
• The lack of access to education for the majority of the population contributed to income disparities, as literacy and skills were concentrated among the elite.
 
• Unequal wage distribution across sectors, such as agriculture and industrial labor, further exacerbated the economic divide.
 
• Limited irrigation and infrastructure investments in rural areas led to low agricultural productivity, which was a significant contributor to rural poverty.
 
 
 
• **Permanent Settlement System:**
 
 
• Implemented by the British in 1793, this system fixed the land revenue that landlords had to pay to the colonial government.
 
• Landlords were granted ownership rights to vast tracts of land, while tenant farmers had little to no rights and were heavily exploited.
 
 
 
• **Ryotwari System:**
 
 
• In areas like Madras and Bombay, the Ryotwari system allowed direct revenue collection from individual farmers.
 
• However, high taxation rates under this system pushed farmers into poverty and debt.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Economic Impacts of Unequal Land Ownership:**

 
 
• Unequal land ownership patterns led to the concentration of wealth among landlords and systemic poverty among tenant farmers.
 
• Such disparities hindered agricultural development and contributed to frequent famines and food shortages during colonial rule.
 
 
 
• **Social Impacts:**
 
 
• Economic inequality reinforced social hierarchies and caste-based discrimination, as land ownership was often tied to caste privilege.
 
• It restricted upward mobility for marginalized communities and perpetuated generational poverty.
 
 
 
• **Post-Independence Reforms:**
 
 
• After independence, land reforms such as land redistribution and abolition of the zamindari system were initiated to address these inequalities.
 
• However, the implementation of these reforms varied across states, and issues of land inequality persist in modern India.
